seo.meta_title: 받아먹다, 사 먹다, 잡아먹다 | Korean Double Verbs AI Misreads
seo.meta_description: AI reads 받아먹다 as 'receive and eat'. In Korean double verbs, the first verb says how the second happens — and many have a figurative meaning.

ai_failure.situation: You read 아기가 이유식을 잘 받아먹어요 on a parenting blog, then 뇌물을 받아먹었다 in a news headline.
ai_failure.ai_mistake: Translates both literally as 'receive and eat', so the news reads as 'he received and ate a bribe'.
ai_failure.why_it_fails: In a double verb, the first verb sets up how the second happens. 받아먹다 is eating what someone feeds you — a baby taking a spoon, a dog catching a treat. Figuratively, it means pocketing money or favors, and it's negative.

natural_solution.rule: Read the first verb as 'how' and the second as 'what'. Then check whether the pair has a figurative meaning in news, dramas or lyrics.

alternatives.context: 'The baby eats well when fed' — the literal, everyday use
'I bought my lunch' (ate out) vs 'I cooked it myself'. English just says 'I had lunch'.
Literally 'catch and eat' (a predator). Figuratively 'eat someone alive': 잡아먹을 듯이 쳐다봤어 — 'glared like he'd eat me'.
'I'll bring it to you' (polite). Three verbs — take, carry, give — in one.

nuance: English uses one verb plus a preposition ('bring over', 'eat out'). Korean chains verbs instead: 들고 가다 (carry and go), 찾아오다 (look for and come = visit), 뛰어가다 (run and go). Most are transparent once you read them as 'how + what'. The tricky ones are those that grew a second meaning: 받아먹다 (take bribes), 잡아먹다 (bully, or 'eat up' time and money: 시간을 잡아먹다), 집어먹다 (help yourself, grab a bite). When a double verb shows up in a headline or an argument, assume the figurative meaning first.
